1	/**
2	 * stale-sweep.ts — the watch's sweep: hand a node back when the run that took its turn is
3	 * over and nothing released it.
4	 *
5	 * ## Why a sweep, and why scheduled
6	 *
7	 * Every report a run makes comes from a step INSIDE it, and the outside check for the run
8	 * that never reported is `Atomaton Run Watch` — which fires on `workflow_run: completed`.
9	 * GitHub starts no workflow run for an event its own token triggered, and every runner run
10	 * is dispatched by the machinery with `GITHUB_TOKEN`. So the watch has never seen the runs
11	 * it exists for: measured over its whole history, every reconciliation it performed was of
12	 * an ENTRY run, and none of a runner run. The insurance was pointed away from the risk.
13	 *
14	 * A schedule does not depend on an event being delivered. It asks the question directly —
15	 * "which node still holds a lock whose run is over" — over the nodes wearing the
16	 * in-progress label, which is what a run puts on when it takes the turn and exactly the
17	 * set a dead run leaves behind.
18	 *
19	 * ## What counts as stale
20	 *
21	 * `domain/work/stale-lock.ts` is the judgement and `adapters/github/node-lock.ts` is the
22	 * reads; this module is the loop and the writing. The one thing to keep in view here: the
23	 * release is the SAME ending the watch posts for a single run — a turn-ending header
24	 * answering the claim's ask — so every reader that was waiting for an ending (the guard,
25	 * the aggregation's `parent-busy` check, the next sweep) reads it as one.
26	 *
27	 * A park is released the same way and says something different, because it is a different
28	 * fact: the run did answer (`ended=waiting`), and what never arrived is the collection the
29	 * aggregation was to perform.
30	 *
31	 * ## What it will not do
32	 *
33	 * It writes nothing for a node whose lock is fresh, or whose question could not be
34	 * answered. A sweep with nothing stale makes no writes at all — it reads threads and run
35	 * statuses and stops, which is what makes it safe to run every fifteen minutes.
36	 *
37	 * It also does not end a person's turn for them: a node whose thread holds no claim is not
38	 * this sweep's, whatever its label says.
39	 */

53	 * The notice a claim that outlived its run leaves behind.
54	 *
55	 * The same shape the watch posts for one run, and the same subject: the ASK. What a reader
56	 * needs is that this request went unanswered — the run that took it up is the how. The
57	 * sweep says one more thing the per-run watch does not have to, because it found the node
58	 * by looking for exactly this: the lock had been standing.

36	 * runner sets it, because a pull request run checks out the pull request and its

38	 * reviewing it behaves. See `atomaton-runner.wac.ts`.
39	 *

3	 *
4	 * The claim a run writes at start names it (`atomaton:took=<ask> run=<run>`), and that id
5	 * is the only thing that can answer "is anybody still working here" from outside a run. A
6	 * thread that says an agent holds the turn is telling the truth about who TOOK it and
7	 * nothing about who is still there — a run killed by its context budget, a lost runner, a
8	 * timeout leaves the claim standing and no step inside the run can say so.
9	 *
10	 * `actions/runs/{id}` is the outside answer, and it is the same fact a run's own
11	 * `workflow_run` completion carries — only fetched rather than delivered. That difference
12	 * is the whole point: GitHub starts no workflow run for an event its own token triggered,
13	 * so a runner dispatched by the machinery never fires a `workflow_run` at all, which is why
14	 * the watch that listens for one has never seen the runs it exists for.
15	 *
16	 * Read-only, retried (a `ghRead`), and never throws: a status that could not be read is
17	 * reported as such, and the callers treat it as "not an answer" rather than as "not
18	 * running" — releasing a live run's lock is the harm, so the unreadable case must not
19	 * resolve to it.
20	 */

25	export function readRunStatus(repo: string, runId: number): RunStatusRead {
26	  const read = ghRead("api", `repos/${repo}/actions/runs/${runId}`, "--jq", ".status");
27	  if (read.code !== 0) {
28	    return { read: false, why: (read.stderr || read.stdout || `gh exited ${read.code}`).trim().split("\n")[0] ?? "" };
29	  }
30	  const status = (read.stdout ?? "").trim();
31	  // An empty answer is not a status. GitHub's "resource not accessible" is a 403 and lands
32	  // above; this is the other shape of "nobody told me" — a projection that matched nothing.
33	  // Reading it as a live run would hold a dead lock forever, and reading it as finished
34	  // would release a live one, so it is neither.
35	  if (status === "") return { read: false, why: "the run read returned no status" };
36	  return { read: true, status };

1	# How a run ends, and what a failure leaves behind
2	
3	A run that gets to report ends with exactly one turn-ending comment on the issue or
4	pull request it worked on. That comment is how the thread learns the turn is over —
5	the guard reads the thread, not the Actions tab.
6	
7	## The two ways the comment is written
8	
9	**The agent's own last message.** A run that finishes by saying something has that
10	message posted as the turn-ending comment, footer attached.
11	
12	**A session-ending tool.** `create_pr`, `launch_sub_agent`, `request_close_issue`
13	and `reload_environment` end the session while doing their work, and the comment
14	such a call left on the thread is the ending: the footer is appended onto it, so
15	the run still has exactly one.
16	
17	The footer is the record of a run that reported — the run's link, its token count,
18	its metrics link — and it goes on those two comments and no others. The failure
19	notice below is a turn-ending comment without one: it links the run's log itself,
20	and a run that failed mid-turn has no token tally worth recording.
21	
22	## What the comment calls
23	
24	The comment is also the run's call: it says who holds the work next. A run ends by
25	calling **one thing, or nobody**:
26	
27	- **one agent**, as a line holding nothing but `/` and the agent's name. The lines
28	  after it are the request;
29	- **or one person**, as a single `@login` of somebody the run was told it may call —
30	  a participant in the thread, a collaborator, or whoever the work belongs to;
31	- **or nobody**, and the comment then mentions the person the work belongs to, so
32	  that a turn coming back to a person is not silent.
33	
34	People and agents are peers here: both take the turn, and one of them takes it.
35	Two calls is not a hand-off with a courtesy copy — it is two people who each
36	believe the work is theirs, and it is refused. The run is asked once more, in its
37	own session, and a message that still calls two things is posted with its mentions
38	left as text: nothing in it is started, nobody in it is notified, and the machinery
39	makes the one call it still can by mentioning the person the work belongs to. The
40	comment then carries a warning saying so, so the text is not read as a hand-off
41	that happened.
42	
43	A run that was cut short never made a call either — its last message is a fragment
44	of the work — so every mention in a salvaged fragment is escaped as well, and the
45	machinery's mention is what reaches a person.
46	
47	## A failure that gets reported is also an ending
48	
49	When the agent itself fails, the failure is converted into the comment it owed the
50	thread. The failure notice IS the turn-ending comment: it says the session was
51	saved, names the two ways forward — continue with `/agent`, or start clean with
52	`/agent recover` — and links the run's log. The node is back with a person, so the
53	next comment on the thread resumes normally.
54	
55	**One step posts it, whatever the run did.** There used to be two writers, and which
56	one ran depended on whether the step the agent ran in succeeded: a run whose step
57	succeeded and whose core filed `failed` reached the result comment, and a run whose
58	step exited non-zero reached a separate "Report failure" step, because nothing later
59	in the run would have. One event with two writers, each reachable only through a
60	signal the other could not see — and the cost was a run that fell between them: the
61	step succeeded, the core filed `failed`, and the thread got nothing at all. No
62	comment, no `atomaton:ended`, and a person with no way to learn anything but by
63	opening the run and reading its log.
64	
65	So the result-comment step now runs for both outcomes, and reads the step's own
66	outcome. A step that failed with no ending recorded *is* a failed run, and the same
67	notice the core's `failed` produced is what it posts: what did not finish, that the
68	session is saved, the two ways forward, and the tail of the run's log — under the
69	`atomaton:ended` tag every ending carries, so the thread's guard comes off and the
70	next comment resumes normally.
71	
72	Four shapes still post nothing, and each should. A run that never claimed the turn owes
73	the thread nothing. A run that found no events never reached the agent at all. A
74	cancelled run is a person stopping it on purpose, and its half-written output is not a
75	report. And a run whose agent step was *skipped* is a machinery death before the agent
76	started — the one the run watch below exists for, because the report from inside the
77	run could not happen.
78	
79	The colour follows what the comment says, because the thing that reports is a step
80	inside the run:
81	
82	- **The agent's own failure, reported — green.** The notice is the run's report;
83	  a red run beside it would only repeat that news in Notifications, where it
84	  drowns the runs whose red is their only signal.
85	- **The machinery's failure — red, ending or not.** A machinery failure inside the
86	  run itself (the tools file it could not write, a `sudo` it was refused, an
87	  ending it could not read) still posts the notice, so the thread is healed — but
88	  the run goes red, because red is the machinery's signal and the thread is healed
89	  beside it, not instead of it.
90	- **A failure that could not be reported — red, and no ending.** The machinery
91	  died before the reporter could run (the checkout, the tool installs, the session
92	  save), or `gh` refused the comment. Red is then the only signal the run leaves,
93	  and the workflow log says what the thread does not.
94	
95	Whose a failure was is read off one flag, which the agent's step writes only when
96	`atoma` itself exits with a failure and nothing else writes. A flag that is absent
97	reads as the machinery's, so losing it turns every failure red again — the
98	conservative direction, since the notice posts either way.
99	
100	## When a run leaves no ending at all
101	
102	A run that died before it could report — the third case above — leaves the
103	thread's last turn event saying the ball is still with an agent. The guard reads
104	that the same way it reads a live run —
105	[what keeps two runs off one issue](what-keeps-two-runs-off-one-issue.md) — so it
106	keeps removing what a person writes next, and it suppresses the dispatch as well:
107	no run arrives to heal the thread. Comments that keep vanishing with no run behind
108	them are this shape.
109	
110	**The run watch is the outside check for exactly this.** When a run completes,
111	`Atomaton Run Watch` reads the node's thread and asks one question of the turn's
112	own identity: does the thread hold a claim by this run — `atomaton:took`, written
113	when the run started — and no ending by this run — `atomaton:ended`, which every
114	report carries? A run that reported has the ending, and the watch stays silent. A
115	run that claimed and never reported gets a notice: the turn-ending header that
116	closes the ask the run claimed, the fact that nothing was decided, the run's link,
117	and the two ways forward. The notice is itself that ending — it carries the ask's
118	id and the watch's own run id — so the ask reads as answered after it, and no
119	later watch posts the same notice twice: once per ask is the whole of what the
120	residue of a dead run owes. The watch also removes the `atomaton/in-progress`
121	label the dead run left, by the same turn rule the runner itself applies. It
122	cannot double-post against the run's own report: the watched run's completion
123	fires only after its own steps are done, so a report that landed at all landed
124	first.
125	
126	The claim is what makes the watch's question answerable at all. Before it
127	existed, the thread said that SOMETHING was asked for but not who had taken it up,
128	and the watch estimated the answer from timestamps and event shapes — and

129	estimated wrong twice, both times notifying a run that was still working. Now the

138	
139	The watch reads which node a run worked on out of the run's title. The runner
140	writes `run-name: "agent on #N"`; the two entry workflows write `#N` alone,
141	because `run-name` is evaluated before any job runs and the agent is a route's

147	runner were still to come. The PR chain is watched through the runner run that
148	validation eventually starts, whose title carries the agent. Titles matching
149	neither shape — runs from before this existed — are left alone.
150	
151	The restore is the same for every kind of death: **re-run the failed run**.
152	"Re-run failed jobs" from the run's page, or by hand:
153	
154	```bash
155	gh workflow run atomaton-runner.yml -f number=N -f agent=X -f type=issue
156	```
157	
158	The job runs again from the saved session and writes the ending it owed — and once
159	the ending is on the thread, comments go through again. The watch is what makes
160	the thread survivable in the meantime; only the re-run makes the work continue.
161	Three deaths it cannot cover, because nothing outside GitHub can: GitHub itself
162	down (nobody can write anything), a run queued forever (its completion never
163	fires), and a deleted node (nowhere to post). There the red run is the only
164	signal, and re-running it is the recovery.

25	 * error surfaced anywhere.
